



A 3D rotation can be written using a single unit quaternion $q$ acting on a vector $v$ (embedded as a pure quaternion) via:

$$v' = qvq^{-1}$$

This works because conjugation by a unit quaternion preserves the "vector part" structure and gives you exactly the rotation group $SO(3)$, double-covered by the unit quaternions $S^3$.

**4D rotations need two quaternions, not one.** The group of rotations in 4D, $SO(4)$, turns out to be generated by pairs of unit quaternions $(p, q)$ acting on a 4D vector $x$ (now treated as a full quaternion, not just a pure one) via:

$$x' = p\,x\,q^{-1}$$

This is sometimes called the **isoclinic rotation** representation. A few key facts fall out of this:

- Left multiplication ($x' = px$) and right multiplication ($x' = xq^{-1}$) are themselves each 4D rotations, and they commute with each other.
- Every rotation in $SO(4)$ can be decomposed into a pair of independent "isoclinic" rotations — one purely left-multiplied, one purely right-multiplied — each behaving like a simple rotation in an orthogonal pair of 2-planes.
- The map $(p,q) \mapsto (x \mapsto pxq^{-1})$ gives a 2-to-1 homomorphism from $S^3 \times S^3$ onto $SO(4)$, analogous to how a single unit quaternion double-covers $SO(3)$. This reflects the Lie group isomorphism $Spin(4) \cong SU(2) \times SU(2)$.
- If you set $p = q$, you recover the ordinary 3D rotation formula acting on the pure-quaternion subspace, fixing the real axis — so 3D rotations are the special case of 4D rotations where the two quaternions coincide.
- If $p$ and $q$ are independent, the rotation genuinely mixes the 4th dimension with the other three, which is why 4D rotations feel so much stranger than 3D ones — there are two independent rotation angles/planes rather than one axis.

This two-quaternion structure is exactly why 4D rotations are harder to visualize than 3D ones: instead of one axis and one angle, you have two completely independent invariant planes, each with its own rotation angle, and generic rotations don't have a fixed axis (line) at all — only two fixed orthogonal planes.
